70-085.note: Use pressure altitude, temperature deviation, and RPM row.

why: 550 NM is beyond the chart result for 55% power at 2000 ft and 22°C.
480 NM is too low for the PFP-013 curve intersection.
450 NM substantially under-reads the chart.
Following OAT to PA 2000 ft, then 55% power, gives about 500 NM.
70-086.note: Lower power generally produces greater range in the range chart.

why: 96 kt over-reads the chart at 6000 ft, 10°C, and 65% power.
PFP-014 gives TAS about 92 kt at the specified OAT, PA, and 65% line.
88 kt under-reads the chart.
100 kt is too high for these conditions.
70-087.note: Read OAT to PA, then horizontally to the selected power line.

why: At 8000 ft and −2°C on the 75% line, PFP-014 gives about 104 kt.
100 kt under-reads the plotted TAS.
95 kt is too low for the stated conditions.
110 kt over-reads the chart.
70-088.note: Use the pressure-altitude line, not indicated altitude.

why: At PA 9000 ft and OAT 12°C, the PFP-011 chart gives maximum ROC about 200 ft/min.
250 ft/min is above the chart value.
350 ft/min is too high for the altitude and temperature.
300 ft/min overstates the chart reading.

why: PFP-011 gives about 480 ft/min at 6500 ft and 0°C.
400 ft/min under-reads the chart.
520 ft/min over-reads the chart.
800 ft/min is far too high for this altitude.
70-090.note: Interpolate between chart lines when the altitude is between marks.

why: 17 L/h and 81 kt are below the chart’s 60% interpolation.
17.5 L/h and 83 kt are not the PFP-014 values.
20 L/h and 89 kt correspond to higher power, not 60%.
At FL85 and −25°C, TAS is about 85 kt; interpolating between 55%/17 and 65%/20 gives 18.5 L/h.
70-091.note: Interpolate the 60% fuel flow between adjacent power lines.

why: PFP-023 top-altitude cumulative fuel minus FL65 cumulative fuel gives 1 gallon.
2 gallons is not the difference between the two chart readings.
6 gallons greatly overstates the required climb fuel.
3 gallons is not the top-minus-start chart difference.
70-092.note: For climbs starting above sea level, subtract cumulative chart values.

why: The chart distance from FL65 to FL95 is 6 NM; it is the upper-altitude value minus the lower-altitude value.
3 NM under-reads the cumulative distance difference.
16 NM incorrectly uses a much larger climb interval.
10 NM is not the FL65-to-FL95 chart difference.
70-093.note: Subtract chart values at start altitude from values at destination altitude.

why: Interception lines are not a range-limit depiction.
They do not authorize continuing VFR below visibility minima.
They are not simply a list of nearby airports.
Interception lines provide recognizable guidance to help regain orientation if lost.
70-094.note: Use preplanned visual lines to recover situational awareness.

why: VFR semicircular levels are based on magnetic course, not true course.
Magnetic heading includes wind correction; the rule uses course.
VFR semicircular rules use magnetic course.
True heading is not the reference for selecting the semicircular level.
70-095.note: Convert to magnetic course, then apply the VFR level rule.

why: FL150 is not the upper limit printed for LO R 16.
The chart gives the limit in feet MSL, not metres.
LO R 16’s upper limit is 1500 ft MSL.
The reference is MSL, not height above ground.
70-096.note: Read the restriction limit and its vertical datum carefully.

why: 4500 ft AGL is not the charted upper limit; the datum is MSL.
LO R 4 upper limit is 4500 ft MSL.
1500 ft MSL is the wrong value for this restricted area.
4500 ft AGL uses the wrong reference datum.
70-097.note: MSL and AGL are not interchangeable; use the chart notation.

why: 75 L adds taxi, alternate, and reserve, which are not trip fuel.
52 L incorrectly includes non-trip fuel components or mis-adds the phases.
49 L includes more than trip fuel; taxi, parking, alternate, and reserve are excluded.
Trip fuel is climb + cruise + descent: 12 + 25 + 7 = 44 L.
70-098.note: Trip fuel excludes taxi, alternate, contingency, and final reserve.

why: A strong tailwind changes the optimum TAS slightly; it is not exactly the still-air maximum-range TAS.
This confuses maximum endurance with range and predicts a large reduction.
For maximum range into a strong tailwind, the optimum TAS is slightly lower than in still air.
A tailwind does not require slightly higher TAS for maximum endurance.
70-099.note: Adjust range speed downward in tailwind and upward in headwind.

why: The destination fuel includes the 30% reserve; it is not 80 kg.
40 kg is not the result of doubling fuel used in the first half and subtracting from 180.
10 kg ignores the stated reserve-inclusive starting fuel and projected trip burn.
After half the distance 80 kg was used; projected total trip burn is 160 kg, leaving 20 kg at destination.
70-100.note: At unchanged conditions, double first-half burn to estimate total trip burn.

why: After protecting 20 USG reserve, 60 USG remains for 2 h 20 min; 60/2.333 = 25.7 USG/h.
42.9 USG/h spends too much fuel and fails to preserve reserve.
25.7 USG/h is the maximum flow: (80−20) ÷ (2+20/60).
34.3 USG/h is above the allowable rate if 20 USG reserve must remain.
70-101.note: Subtract reserve, then divide usable fuel by remaining time.

why: 145 kt and 71.1 GPH do not match the CAP697 3400-lb, FL75, 23 in/2300 RPM entry; GPH is implausibly high.
160 kt is the chart TAS, but 12.3 GPH is not the matching fuel flow.
At FL75 and ISA, the table gives TAS 160 kt and FF 11.9 GPH.
145 kt is the wrong speed; the table gives 160 kt, and 11.9 GPH is paired with it.
70-102.note: Read the correct pressure-altitude and power row in CAP697.

why: At FL65 and ISA+20, CAP697 gives IAS 142 kt and fuel flow 11.5 GPH.
145 kt and 11.9 GPH are not the table values at the specified temperature.
158 kt is not IAS for this setting; it overstates the table speed.
150 kt and 12.3 GPH are not the listed conditions’ values.
70-103.note: Distinguish IAS from TAS and use the specified temperature column.

why: 15 USG extra would imply 35 USG at landing, but projected total trip burn is 80, leaving only 15 total.
5 USG extra is inconsistent with the arithmetic; only 15 USG remains against 20 USG required.
40 USG is not the landing total after projecting burn for the full distance.
Halfway consumption is 40, so total trip burn is 80; 95−80 = 15 USG, below the 20-USG alternate/reserve requirement.
70-104.note: Compare projected destination fuel with protected reserve fuel.

why: Trip burn projects to 60 USG; 90−60 = 30 at landing, which exceeds the 20-USG protected fuel.
30 USG remains at landing in total, so it is not 30 in addition to the reserve.
Projected burn is 2×30 = 60; landing fuel 90−60 = 30, less 20 reserve = 10 USG extra.
10 USG is the amount above reserve, not total landing fuel.
70-105.note: Fuel remaining above reserve = destination fuel − alternate/final reserve.

why: Lower temperature increases air density, which generally increases piston-engine power; the statement reverses the effect.
Higher temperature means lower density and less oxygen per volume, reducing piston-engine power.
Higher temperature reduces density rather than increasing it.
Lower temperature does not reduce density; it increases density and generally power.
70-106.note: Hot, high conditions reduce density and piston-engine output.
